beats.narration_text: Hi, I'm Om Mali. This video is about joining two different S E C filings together, so that a private company's funding round and the day a mutual fund actually bought into it can be lined up against each other. Until now this project worked from one form, which says what a position is worth but never when it was bought. This week I added two that do.

props.segment: Joining Filed Rounds to Fund Entry Dates
props.command: Bring in Form D for offering dates and the restricted-securities footnote for acquisition dates, and join them to the marks panel. Do not key the join on a company name — tell me what breaks if I do.
output: a name scan returns 706 rows — 84% of them are feeder funds, not the company
footnote parser: 249 positions, 227 with a position cost, entry dates back to 2015-01-20
and 10 of 18 fund entry dates land on the exact day an issuer reported a sale

beats.narration_text: Two new filings, beside the panel. Form D, which a company files when it sells shares, gives offering dates and amounts. The restricted securities footnote in a fund's annual report gives acquisition dates and cost. Joining them is the week. And the join does not run on a company name. It runs on an identifier a person confirmed.

shot.visual_intent: The BLUF names both sources by WHO files them, because that asymmetry is what makes B07's agreement evidence rather than arithmetic.

show.event: The headline sets, then the two source cards land side by side.
Each card fills in who files it, what it gives, and how much of it there is.

show.at: on 'does not run on a company name'
show.event: A 'a name' chip lands as the join key and is struck through.
The real key replaces it beneath.

beats.narration_text: Here is why. The obvious way to find a company's Form D filings is to search for its name. I did that across forty-nine quarters and got seven hundred and six rows. Five hundred and ninety-five of them, about eighty-four percent, are not the company. They are feeder funds named after it, raising money to buy its shares on the secondary market.

shot.visual_intent: Rebuild of pantry/w9-nametrap.png. The feeder share has to LOOK like the majority, because the whole join design follows from it being one.

show.event: One full-width bar draws and the total counts up to 706.
The bar splits — the feeder share takes the accent and dominates the frame.
A REAL feeder name lands beneath, with what it actually is.

props.sparkLine: Eighty-four percent are not the company.
props.title: What a name scan actually returns
props.subtitle: 49 quarters, 2014q1 → 2026q1
props.example: Anthropic Jan 2026 a Series of CGF2021 LLC
props.exampleNote: A fund raising money to buy Anthropic shares on the secondary market. The amount it sold is its own raise, not Anthropic's.
props.archiveNote: 2008Q2-2013Q4 are not published by the SEC; 2008Q1 and 2012Q1 exist as orphans and are deliberately excluded so that the earliest observed filing is a property of a contiguous archive rather than of which orphan a company happened to appear in.

beats.narration_text: The amount a feeder sold is its own raise. Add those up, call it a funding round, and you have published numbers no company ever filed. So the join runs on an EDGAR identifier a person has confirmed. The code proposes, a human decides. That mattered. One filer from twenty fourteen normalises to exactly the same string as X dot A I, and is a completely different company.

shot.visual_intent: The collision is the argument's teeth: it shows that no better string normalisation would have helped, which is what justifies a human in the loop.

beats.narration_text: The second source has no bulk dataset and no required format. The regulation says what must be disclosed, not what the columns are called, so every fund family writes it differently. Four use tables with different headings. One uses no table at all. That got me two hundred and forty-nine positions, two hundred and twenty-seven with a cost.

beats.narration_text: Two things the marks panel could not say before. The first is when a fund actually bought. Entry dates reach back to January twenty fifteen, nearly eight years before the panel's first observation of that company. But only three of the seven companies genuinely reach back. For the rest I have only the latest reports, so this is a floor, not a history.

beats.narration_text: The second is an exposure map. Who holds what, and how much of their fund it is, using each filer's own percentage of net assets. Ninety manager and company pairs, across thirty managers and ten companies. This is concentration, not conviction. A large percentage is a fact about the fund's size as much as about the position.

beats.narration_text: Then the part I did not expect. With both sources joined, ten of eighteen fund acquisition dates fall on the exact day a company reported selling shares. The clearest case is Databricks, October twenty nineteen. Five separate fund managers independently name that same day. The company files because it sold. The funds file because they own. Neither cites the other.

shot.visual_intent: Rebuild of pantry/w9-corroborate.png. The independence of the two filings is the claim, so it is spelled out rather than implied by the count.

show.event: Eighteen dates land on a gap-days axis; the ten at zero stack at the origin.
That row lifts out with its five registrants.
Three lines land explaining why the agreement is independent.

props.title: 10 of 18 land on the exact day
props.subtitle: distance from a fund's acquisition date to the nearest filed round
props.chartNote: the dark dot above the stack is 1 day away, not zero
props.caseNote: The company filed saying it sold $400M of stock. 5 separate fund managers independently name that same day.
props.whyLabel: why this is evidence and not arithmetic
why: The company files because it SOLD.
The funds file because they OWN.
props.caveat: Agreement is evidence, not proof of causation: a fund buying on the day an issuer reports first sale is consistent with participating in that round, and also with a secondary purchase that happened to settle the same day. What it is not is circular — neither filing cites the other.
props.source: SOURCE: figdata_week9.json — corroboration.pairs[], corroboration.caveat. The $400M offering amount is not in figdata_week9.json — from narration_script.md and the filing itself.

beats.narration_text: One caution, and it is the whole number. That fifty-six percent counts only purchases made while a company was still filing. One company stopped in mid twenty twenty-two, and most of its later buys have no round to match. Count those and fifty-six percent reads as thirty-three. The denominator is doing the work.

shot.visual_intent: The same numerator under two denominators, side by side — the reel ends by showing how easily its own headline could be restated.

props.sparkLine: The denominator is doing the work.
props.title: The same ten hits, two denominators
props.outsideLabel: dates with no round to match
props.whyNote: One company stopped filing Form D in mid-2022. Its later purchases have no round to be near, so the distance to the nearest one measures the end of the archive, not the behaviour of a fund.
notShown: No valuation. Neither source carries shares outstanding, so nothing divides to a company value.
No return. A footnote cost over a later mark is not one — the share count may have changed between them.
Agreement is evidence, not causation. A same-day buy is equally consistent with a secondary purchase that settled that day.

beats.narration_text: Week nine on one page. Two new filings joined to the panel. A name scan returns seven hundred and six rows of which eighty-four percent are feeder funds, so the join runs on a confirmed identifier instead. Five layouts of the same footnote gave two hundred and forty-nine positions and entry dates back to twenty fifteen. Ten of eighteen entry dates land on the exact day a company reported a sale, and that is evidence rather than causation. Counted against every date instead, fifty-six percent reads as thirty-three.

show.event: The Claude artifact page opens — Joining Filed Rounds to Fund Entry Dates, week 9.
Five findings stagger in, one per spoken clause.

props.artifactTitle: Joining Filed Rounds to Fund Entry Dates — week 9
artifactLines: Two sources added beside N-PORT: Form D (706 rows over 49 quarters) for offering dates, and the Reg S-X 12-12 footnote (249 positions from 31 filings) for acquisition dates and cost.

A name scan is 84% wrong: 595 of 706 matches are feeder vehicles raising money to buy the company's shares, not the company. The join runs on a confirmed EDGAR identifier — and one 2014 filer normalises to the same string as X.AI.
Five layouts for one footnote, because the rule names what must be disclosed and not what the columns are called. 227 of 249 positions carry a position cost; the other 22 report cost at fund level.
Entry dates reach to 2015-01-20, 7.9 years before that company's first mark — but only 3 of 7 companies genuinely predate the panel, so this is a floor and not a history.
10 of 18 acquisition dates fall on the exact day an issuer reported a sale (56%) — evidence, not causation, and neither filing cites the other. Against all 30 dates it is 33%.

beats.narration_text: Your turn. Paste this into Claude. Find a join in your own data that runs on a name or a label rather than an identifier. Then count how many of its matches are actually the thing you meant. Not a sample, a count. Mine was sixteen percent, and I only found out because I looked at what the other eighty-four were.

For each one, count what share of the matches are actually the entity I meant — a count, not a sample — and show me the ones that are not. Then tell me which of them no amount of string normalisation would fix.
